t: Article 368 (Part XX) governs the amendment powers and procedure of the Indian Constitution, balancing flexibility and rigidity.
3 Methods of Amendment: Simple Majority (Outside Art. 368): Creation/alteration of States (Art. 3), creation/abolition of State Legislative Councils (Art. 169), salaries of judges/officials.
3 Methods of Amendment: Special Majority (Under Art. 368): Passed by each House separately by a majority of the total membership + 2/3 of members present and voting.

3 Methods of Amendment: Special Majority + Ratification by ≥ 1/2 State Legislatures: Required for federal provisions (e.g., Presidential election, Union/State executive & legislative relations, Supreme Court & High Courts, 7th Schedule Lists, Art. 368 itself, GST Council).
Initiation: Constitution Amendment Bill can originate in either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha (cannot be introduced in State Legislatures).
Prior Recommendation: Prior recommendation of the President is NOT required.
No Joint Sitting: Each House must pass the Bill independently with special majority; if one House rejects it, the Bill fails completely.
Presidential Assent: President must give assent (no veto/return power; made mandatory via 24th Amendment, 1971).

Federal Ratification List: Requires ratification by simple majority of ≥ 1/2 States (not all States). First amendment requiring State ratification was the 3rd Amendment, 1954 (Entry 33, Concurrent List).
Trap: Qualifications, conditions of office, and tenure of the President do NOT require State ratification.

c: Added 9th Schedule, Arts. 31A, 31B, 15(4); protected agrarian/land reforms from judicial review.
Affirmed Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights; made President’s assent compulsory.
Abolished Privy Purses and privileges of former princely state rulers.

"Mini Constitution"; added Socialist, Secular, Integrity to Preamble; added Part IVA (Art. 51A) with 10 Fundamental Duties; added DPSPs 39A, 43A; shifted Education to Concurrent List; added Part XIV-A.
Removed Right to Property from FRs (Art. 300A legal right); replaced "internal disturbance" with "armed rebellion"; President can return advice of Council of Ministers once for reconsideration.
Introduced Anti-Defection Law; inserted the 10th Schedule (amended Arts. 101, 102, 190, 191).
Reduced voting age from 21 years to 18 years (Art. 326).
Conferred special status on Delhi as the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi (Art. 239AA).
Constitutional status to Panchayati Raj; added Part IX (Arts. 243–243O) & 11th Schedule (29 subjects); ≥ 1/3 reservation for women; SFC (Art. 243I) & SEC (Art. 243K).
Constitutional status to Municipalities; added Part IX-A (Arts. 243P–243ZG) & 12th Schedule (18 subjects).
Froze readjustment/allocation of Lok Sabha and State Assembly seats based on 1971 Census up to 2026.
Added Art. 21A (Right to Free & Compulsory Education for ages 6–14); modified Art. 45; added Art. 51A(k) (11th Fundamental Duty).
Bifurcated National Commission for SCs/STs into NCSC (Art. 338) and NCST (Art. 338A).
Capped Council of Ministers at max 15% of Lok Sabha / Legislative Assembly strength (Arts. 75(1A), 164(1A)); barred defectors from ministerial posts.
Provided 27% OBC reservation in educational institutions (Art. 15(5)).
Added right to form Co-operative Societies (Art. 19(1)(c)), DPSP Art. 43B, and Part IX-B (Arts. 243ZH–243ZT; max 21 directors under Art. 243ZJ).
Created NJAC; struck down as unconstitutional by Supreme Court in 2015 for violating judicial independence.
Operationalized India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement (exchange of 111 Indian and 51 Bangladeshi enclaves).
Introduced Goods and Services Tax (GST) effective 1 July 2017; created GST Council (Art. 279A).
Restored power of State Governments and UTs to identify and notify their own SEBCs (Socially and Educationally Backward Classes).

under: Imp Cases: Amendment Power & Basic Structure Chain
t: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973): 13-Judge Bench propounded the Basic Structure Doctrine; held Parliament can amend FRs but cannot alter/destroy the Basic Structure; recognized the Preamble as part of the Constitution.

under: Imp Cases: Amendment Power & Basic Structure Chain
t: Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980): Reinforced the Basic Structure doctrine; struck down clauses giving absolute precedence to DPSPs over FRs; restored the balance between Part III and Part IV.

under: Imp Cases: Key Fundamental Rights & Governance Landmark Cases

under: Imp Cases: Key Fundamental Rights & Governance Landmark Cases

under: Imp Cases: Key Fundamental Rights & Governance Landmark Cases
t: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975): Struck down parts of the 39th Amendment that barred judicial review of election disputes of the PM and Speaker.

under: Imp Cases: Key Fundamental Rights & Governance Landmark Cases
t: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978): Widened Article 21 (Right to Travel Abroad); procedure must be "just, fair, and reasonable"; established the golden triangle (Arts. 14, 19, and 21 are mutually inclusive).

under: Imp Cases: Key Fundamental Rights & Governance Landmark Cases

under: Imp Cases: Key Fundamental Rights & Governance Landmark Cases

t: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): Laid guidelines against arbitrary misuse of Article 356 (President's Rule); made proclamation subject to judicial review; held secularism and federalism as basic features; reaffirmed Preamble as an integral part.

Constitutional Status: Permanent, independent, constitutional body under Part XV (Articles 324–329).
Established on 25 January 1950 (celebrated annually as National Voters' Day since 2011).
Article 324(1): Vests the superintendence, direction, and control of elections in the Election Commission of India (ECI).
Mandate covers elections to: Parliament (Lok Sabha & Rajya Sabha), State Legislatures (Assemblies & Councils), President, and Vice-President.
Local body elections (Panchayats and Municipalities) are NOT conducted by ECI; they fall under the State Election Commission (SEC) under Articles 243K & 243ZA.

Composition: 1 Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) + 2 Election Commissioners (multi-member body established continuously since 1 October 1993). All three have equal powers, salary equivalent to Supreme Court Judges, and decide by majority.
Appointment: By the President of India.
Tenure: 6 years or up to 65 years of age, whichever is earlier.
Removal Safeguards: CEC: Removed only in like manner and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court Judge (Art. 324(5)).
Removal Safeguards: Other ECs & Regional Commissioners: Removed by the President on the recommendation of the CEC.

Constitutional Status: Permanent, independent, quasi-judicial constitutional body under Article 280 (Part XII).
Constituted by the President of India every 5 years or earlier as deemed necessary (not strictly/rigidly every 5 years).
First Commission: Constituted under Presidential order in 1951, set up on 6 April 1952 under Chairman K.C. Neogy.
Core Function: Anchor of Fiscal Federalism; recommends the distribution of net tax proceeds between the Union and States, and the allocation among States.
Composition (Art. 280(1)): Total 5 members -> 1 Chairman + 4 other members appointed by the President.
Qualifications (Art. 280(2)): Determined by Parliament by law (NOT determined by the President or Union Cabinet).
Nature: Possesses powers of a civil court regarding summoning and production of documents (quasi-judicial character).
Devolution of Taxes: Distribution of the net proceeds of divisible Union taxes between Centre and States, and allocation among States.
Grants-in-Aid: Principles governing grants-in-aid of State revenues out of the Consolidated Fund of India (Art. 275).

Local Bodies Resource Augmentation: Measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of a State to supplement the resources of Panchayats and Municipalities based on recommendations of the State Finance Commission.
Sound Finance: Any other matter referred to it by the President in the interest of sound public finance.

Submission of Report (Art. 281): Submits its report to the President, who causes it to be laid before both Houses of Parliament along with an explanatory memorandum on action taken (Trap: Report is laid by the President, NOT the Finance Minister).

under: Lok Sabha: Rules of Procedure & Conduct of Business
t: Primary mechanisms for executive accountability: Question Hour, Supplementary Questions, and Adjournment Motions.
No-Confidence Motion (Rule 198): Not mentioned in the Constitution; introduced ONLY in Lok Sabha.
No-Confidence Motion (Rule 198): Moved against the entire Council of Ministers (cannot be moved against an individual minister).
No-Confidence Motion (Rule 198): Requires written notice to the Secretary-General and the support of at least 50 members for leave to be granted.
Confidence Motion: Moved by the Council of Ministers/Government to demonstrate majority support on the floor.
Rule 184 (Discussion + Voting): Permits discussion on a specific matter of public interest followed by voting (carries significant political consequences for the government).

Rule 377 (Special Mention of Matters): Allows members to raise matters of general public importance that cannot be raised under rules governing Questions, Calling Attention, or other formal Motions; requires written notice and Speaker's consent (increased from 20 to 30 matters/day in 2015).
Rule 8(1): Governs the procedure for the election of the Deputy Speaker (date fixed by the Speaker and notified by the Secretary-General).

t: Starred Question: Requires an oral answer on the floor; supplementary questions are ALLOWED (max 20 starred questions listed for oral answer per day).
Unstarred Question: Requires a written answer laid on the table; supplementary questions are NOT allowed.
Short Notice Question: Pertains to an urgent matter of public importance; asked with notice shorter than 10 clear days; receives an oral answer; supplementary questions are ALLOWED.
Adjournment Motion: Interrupts normal business to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance and recent occurrence.
Adjournment Motion: Involves an element of censure/condemnation against the government.
Calling Attention Motion: Indian parliamentary innovation to draw the attention of a Minister to an urgent matter of public importance.
Calling Attention Motion: Resembles an Adjournment Motion but does NOT contain an element of censure/condemnation.
Closure Motion & Guillotine: Closure Motion: Moved to cut short debate and put the question to vote.
Closure Motion & Guillotine: Guillotine: A form of closure applied when allotted time expires all remaining discussed and undiscussed clauses/demands are immediately put to vote.
Article vs Rule Matching: No-Confidence Motion: Lok Sabha Rule 198 (NOT an Article).
Article vs Rule Matching: Rule 184: Substantive motion requiring discussion with voting.
Article vs Rule Matching: Money Bill / Joint Sitting: Constitutional (Arts. 110 & 108).
Negative Traps: Zero Hour is NOT a constitutional provision.
Negative Traps: No-Confidence Motion can NOT be moved in Rajya Sabha.
Negative Traps: Unstarred questions do NOT allow supplementary questions.
Negative Traps: Calling Attention does NOT carry censure/condemnation against the government.

t: Original Jurisdiction (Art. 131): Exclusive jurisdiction over federal disputes (Centre ↔ State or State ↔ State). Does not cover pre-Constitution treaties or inter-State water disputes (Art. 262).

Acting CJI vs Ad Hoc Judge: Acting CJI (Art. 126): Appointed by the President when the CJI is unable to perform duties.
Acting CJI vs Ad Hoc Judge: Ad Hoc Judge (Art. 127): Appointed by the CJI (with previous consent of the President and consultation with the concerned HC Chief Justice) to meet a lack of quorum.
Removal vs Appointment: The President appoints SC judges in consultation/collegium concurrence, but removal requires a statutory inquiry + parliamentary special majority address under Art. 124(4).
Court of Record (Art. 129): Judgments have evidentiary value and cannot be questioned when produced before any subordinate court; includes power to punish for contempt.
Constitutional Status: Highest law officer of the Government of India under Part V (Article 76).
Appointment: Appointed by the President of India.
Tenure: Holds office during the pleasure of the President (No fixed constitutional tenure).
Removal & Resignation: Can be removed at any time by the President; resignation is submitted to the President (traditionally resigns when the Council of Ministers changes).
Remuneration: Determined by the President (not fixed by Parliament or the Constitution).
Primary Role: Advises the Government of India on legal matters and performs other legal duties referred by the President.

Qualifications (Equivalent to a Supreme Court Judge): Must be a citizen of India, AND; Has been a High Court Judge for at least 5 years, OR; Has been an advocate of a High Court for at least 10 years, OR; Is a distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President.
Right of Audience: Enjoys the right of audience in all courts within the territory of India while performing official duties.
